mcqs.question: What is the 'power wall' that stopped CPU clock speeds from climbing further around the mid-2000s?
options: A legal limit imposed on how fast CPUs are allowed to run
Software stopped requiring any additional performance
Manufacturers ran out of ways to shrink transistors further
Dynamic power scales with frequency and voltage squared, so pushing clock speed higher makes power and heat grow far faster than the resulting performance gain, past what chips can dissipate
mcqs.explanation: The power wall is a physical power/heat constraint: power grows super-linearly with frequency (via the voltage-squared term), making further clock increases prohibitively hot and power-hungry. It isn't a legal limit, isn't about transistor shrink running out (Moore's Law continued), and software demand for performance never stopped.

mcqs.question: What defines a symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) system?
options: Every core is identical, shares the same memory, and can run any task interchangeably
One core acts as a manager while all others are dedicated to specific fixed roles
Each core has entirely separate, non-shared physical memory
Only one core is ever active at a time, with others held in reserve
mcqs.explanation: SMP means identical cores sharing memory, with the OS free to run any thread on any core interchangeably — that symmetry is the defining property. A manager-plus-fixed-roles design describes an asymmetric system, separate non-shared memory describes a different architecture entirely (not SMP), and SMP cores run concurrently, not one at a time.

mcqs.question: Why did the shift to multicore end the era of software getting faster 'for free'?
options: Because multicore chips run at a lower clock speed than single-core chips did
Because a single-threaded program doesn't automatically use more than one core, so it sees no speedup on a multicore chip unless it's explicitly rewritten to run in parallel
Because compilers can no longer optimize code for multicore chips
Because multicore chips are only compatible with newly written software
mcqs.explanation: The 'free lunch' was riding rising clock speeds automatically speeding up all existing code; multicore instead requires software to be explicitly restructured into multiple threads to benefit, since a single thread only ever uses one core regardless of how many are available. It's not about clock speed being lower, compiler capability, or backward compatibility, which multicore chips fully retain.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't doubling the number of cores typically double a real program's performance?
options: Because operating systems limit programs to using at most 2 cores
Because doubling core count always halves the clock speed of each core
Because any serial portion of the program caps total speedup (Amdahl's Law) and real workloads also suffer growing contention over shared caches, memory bandwidth, and locks as core count rises
Because compilers refuse to generate code for more than 4 cores
mcqs.explanation: Amdahl's Law shows serial fractions of a program set a hard ceiling on achievable speedup, and rising contention for shared resources (caches, memory bandwidth, locks) further erodes real-world gains as core count grows. There's no OS-imposed 2-core limit, no automatic clock halving from adding cores, and no compiler core-count ceiling of 4.
